claims.claim: ASPREE randomised 19,114 healthy community-dwelling people aged 70 and over (65 and over for US Black and Hispanic participants), without cardiovascular disease, dementia or physical disability, to aspirin 100 mg daily or placebo; its main outcome was disability-free survival (staying alive without dementia or persistent physical disability).
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling persons in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or physical disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg per day of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo orally. The primary end point was a composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability." ... "A total of 19,114 persons with a median age of 74 years were enrolled, of whom 9525 were randomly assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo." Full text (Methods): "The primary end point was disability-free survival, which was defined as survival free from dementia or persistent physical disability." ... "persistent physical disability was considered to have occurred when a participant reported having an inability to perform or severe difficulty in performing at least one of the six basic activities of daily living that had persisted for at least 6 months." ... "the six basic activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, walking, and feeding)"
claims.location: Abstract (Methods, Results); full text Methods (Scite excerpts)
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling, independent people aged 70+ (65+ US Black/Hispanic) in Australia and USA, no CVD, dementia or disability / aspirin 100 mg daily / placebo / death, dementia or persistent physical disability (composite) / median 4.7 years
claims.safe_wording: A trial of daily aspirin in 19,114 healthy people aged 70 and over had one main outcome: staying alive without dementia or lasting disability. 'Lasting disability' meant being unable, or finding it very hard, to do a basic daily task such as washing, dressing, using the toilet or walking, for at least 6 months.
claims.qualifications: Healthy, independent volunteers in Australia and the USA; results do not apply to people who have had a heart attack or stroke. Do not claim that 'most prevention trials' count only heart attacks and strokes: that comparison was not verified. Avoid the negation-then-correction shape when contrasting the outcome with heart attacks and strokes.

minimum duration of ADL loss to count as persistent physical disability
basic activities of daily living assessed

claims.claim: Aspirin did not prolong disability-free survival: over a median 4.7 years the rates were almost identical, and extended follow-up to almost a decade showed no long-term effect.
claims.supporting_passage: PMID 30221596 abstract: "The trial was terminated at a median of 4.7 years of follow-up after a determination was made that there would be no benefit with continued aspirin use with regard to the primary end point. The rate of the composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability was 21.5 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 21.2 per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.01; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.92 to 1.11; P=0.79)." ... "Aspirin use in healthy elderly persons did not prolong disability-free survival over a period of 5 years but led to a higher rate of major hemorrhage than placebo." PMID 41043446 abstract: "Similarly, over the period of both ASPREE and ASPREE-XT, no long-term effect of aspirin versus placebo was observed on the composite outcome of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability over almost a decade of follow-up (HR 1·01; 95% CI 0·95-1·08; p=0·65)"
claims.pico_timeframe: As C07-05-a / aspirin vs placebo / disability-free survival / median 4.7 years in trial; almost a decade including observational extension (15,633 consented)
claims.safe_wording: Aspirin did not help people stay alive and free of dementia and disability. Each year, about 21 in every 1000 people lost that status in both groups. Following people for almost 10 years showed the same.
claims.qualifications: Adherence in the final trial year was 62.1% (aspirin) vs 64.1% (placebo). The trial was stopped early because continuing was judged futile.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found that points the other way for this outcome.

numbers.meaning: events per 1000 person-years, aspirin vs placebo, composite of death, dementia or persistent disability
relative effect over almost a decade including ASPREE-XT

claims.claim: Major haemorrhage was more common with aspirin (3.8% vs 2.8%), and aspirin did not significantly reduce cardiovascular disease.
claims.supporting_passage: PMID 30221596 abstract: "The rate of major hemorrhage was higher in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (3.8% vs. 2.8%; hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)." PMID 30221597 abstract: "After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08). The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001)." PMID 41043446 abstract: "aspirin was associated with an increased hazard for incident major haemorrhagic events across both ASPREE and ASPREE-XT (1·24; 1·10-1·39)."
claims.pico_timeframe: As C07-05-a / aspirin vs placebo / major haemorrhage; cardiovascular disease (fatal CHD, non-fatal MI, stroke, heart failure admission) / median 4.7 years
claims.safe_wording: Over about 5 years, serious bleeding happened to about 4 in 100 people taking aspirin and about 3 in 100 taking the dummy tablet. Heart attacks, strokes and heart failure admissions were not clearly reduced.
claims.qualifications: 3.8% vs 2.8% are cumulative proportions over a median 4.7 years. Say 'did not clearly reduce', not 'no effect', for cardiovascular disease.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None for bleeding. Extended follow-up (not used here) found no long-term cardiovascular benefit either.

cardiovascular disease events per 1000 person-years, aspirin vs placebo (HR 0.95, 0.83 to 1.08)

claims.claim: All-cause mortality was higher with aspirin during the trial, mainly from cancer, a result the authors called unexpected; over almost a decade the difference in deaths was no longer clear.
claims.supporting_passage: PMID 30221595 abstract: "The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29). Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years." ... "In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution." PMID 41043446 abstract: "including no long-term effect on deaths (1·06; 0·99-1·14; p=0·10)." PMID 41609798 abstract: "However, LDA was associated with increased cancer-related mortality (HR = 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03-1.29)."

candidates.reason: All essential claims are supported from ASPREE abstracts and full-text excerpts: design and the disability-free survival outcome with its definition (19,114; aged 70+, 65+ for US Black and Hispanic participants; ADL loss for at least 6 months), no difference in disability-free survival over a median 4.7 years (21.5 vs 21.2 per 1000 person-years) and none over almost a decade (ASPREE-XT), major haemorrhage 3.8% vs 2.8%, and the secondary prevention caveat (ATT 2009; ASPREE excluded CVD). Changes needed: the judge's mortality figures 5.9% vs 5.2% were not found in the sources read and must not be used; if mortality is mentioned, give the trial-period excess (12.7 vs 11.1 per 1000 person-years, authors' caution) together with the extended follow-up showing no clear long-term difference in deaths. Replace PREVENTABLE (not verified) with STAREE (Aug 2026), which also used disability-free survival and found fewer cardiovascular events but no clear gain in disability-free survival. Do not claim 'most prevention trials count heart attacks and strokes' (unverified).

The core point holds but two parts of the evidence differ from the candidate. (1) The age effect is verified for QRISK2, not QRISK3: Ueda 2017 found that even with optimal risk factors men cross 10% between 60 and 70 and women between 65 and 75, and all people aged 75 to 84 without CVD in an English survey sample exceeded 10%. No verified QRISK3 outputs exist for the proposed line chart. Livingstone 2021 (QRISK3, 2.9 million UK records) shows poor discrimination (C <0.65) and over-prediction at 65+. (2) 'Evidence for statins over 75 is thinner' is now outdated: STAREE (NEJM, 29 Aug 2026; 9971 Australians aged 70+, mean 74.7) found atorvastatin 40 mg reduced major cardiovascular events (about 6 vs 8 in 100 over 5.9 years; HR 0.70) but did not clearly lengthen disability-free survival (HR 0.94, 0.84 to 1.05), with similar serious adverse events. NICE NG238 specifics (QRISK3 to 84; atorvastatin 20 mg considered at 85+; statins below 10% by preference) are search_extract only and must stay out unless re-checked.
candidates.revised_angle: By about 75, the QRISK calculator puts almost everyone above the 10% statin line, even people with ideal blood pressure and cholesterol (shown with QRISK2), and in UK records QRISK3 is poor at telling older people's risks apart. So the score cannot settle the decision. The new STAREE trial (2026) answers the next question: in healthy over-70s a statin prevented some heart attacks and strokes (about 6 vs 8 in 100 over 6 years) but did not clearly help people stay alive without dementia or disability. The conversation after 75 is therefore about what the person wants to prevent, how long benefit takes (about 2.5 years per 1 in 100 in younger trials), other illnesses, frailty and preference. Visual: threshold-crossing age bands (QRISK2, labelled) plus STAREE's two outcomes side by side, not a QRISK3 line chart. Coordinate with C07-05 so STAREE is the lead in only one post.

candidates.reason: Ready on the editor's angle. SPRINT exclusions verified verbatim in Williamson 2016 full text (type 2 diabetes, stroke, symptomatic heart failure, dementia, expected survival <3 years, weight loss, standing systolic <110 after 1 minute, nursing home residence), plus the authors' own statement that the over-75 results give no evidence for nursing home residents and people with diabetes, stroke or heart failure. Benefit in over-75s well enough to join: 2.59% vs 3.85% per year, NNT 27 (events) and 41 (deaths) over 3.14 years; serious adverse events 48.4% vs 48.3%; injurious falls 4.9% vs 5.5% (not significant); benefit consistent across frailty strata (exploratory; 30.9% frail). Measurement point verified: unattended automated protocol; routine clinic readings 7.3 and 4.6 mmHg higher (Drawz 2020). 'Trial behind US and European targets' supported (Fernandes 2019) and NICE not adopting lower targets supported (Jones 2020 BJGP summary of NG136). NICE standing BP advice verified. Must carry: Juraschek 2023 (trial benefit similar with orthostatic hypotension) so the post adjusts treatment to standing BP rather than implying a postural drop alone means stopping; Tinetti 2014 is association only. HYVET exclusions not verified and should be left out.

Short-term figures verified (569 randomised, mean age 84.8, GP-selected; systolic <150 at 12 weeks in 86.4% vs 87.7%; 66.3% still reduced at 12 weeks; systolic 3.4 mmHg higher). But the candidate's limitation 'the trial did not measure long-term outcomes' is outdated: a 2024 follow-up (median 4.0 years) found hospitalisation or death in 72% vs 77% (aHR 0.93, 0.76 to 1.12), with about half of surviving intervention participants still on fewer tablets. OPTIMISE2 (about 3000 frail or high-risk people aged 75+) is under way. Not needed as fallback, since C07-03 is ready.
candidates.revised_angle: Open with the question families ask: do all these blood pressure tablets still need taking? In OPTIMISE, GPs stopped one tablet in people aged 80 and over whose pressure was controlled on two or more: at 12 weeks pressure stayed under 150 in 86 in 100 vs 88 in 100 with usual care, and 2 in 3 managed without the tablet. Four years later, hospital admission or death was not clearly different (72 vs 77 in 100) and about half were still on fewer tablets; the result is uncertain enough that a modest harm or benefit cannot be excluded, and a larger trial of frailer people (OPTIMISE2) is under way. Close on a monitored reduction as an option to raise, especially with dizziness or falls.

The practical point should say that stopping and restarting without dummy tablets is a less reliable test (inference from the authors' nocebo discussion); do not claim anything about NHS availability of blinded tests.
